profile.purpose: A list of twelve tips for making better grilled hamburgers. It covers buying and handling the beef, shaping and seasoning patties, grilling technique, doneness, buns and toppings.
profile.thesis: Better burgers come from a set of simple rules: start with fresh, cold, gently handled beef, season only the outside, shape patties for even cooking, grill over a two-zone fire for browning and control, check doneness with a thermometer, and match the bun to the patty.
key_takeaways: Freshly ground beef (e.g. chuck ground by a butcher or supermarket) is looser and juicier than compressed packaged ground beef.
Keep the meat cold so the fat stays in solid chunks and doesn't smear out.
Handle the meat as little as possible; overworking makes a tight, sausage-like patty. Kenji forms patties on parchment without lifting them much.
Don't mix salt or anything else into the meat. Salt draws out moisture and makes the patty tougher, so season only the outside, and liberally, with kosher salt and black pepper.
Make patties a consistent size, using a scale if you want precision, so they cook at the same rate.
Put a dimple in the center of thick patties so they don't bulge as they cook. Press thin patties flat between parchment sheets with a tray.
Use a two-zone fire (coals on one side, or half the gas burners on high) to escape flare-ups and to finish thick burgers on the cooler side with the lid on.
Browning (the Maillard reaction) is flavor. Cook thick burgers on both sides, and thin burgers about 90% on one side.
Use a thermometer: about 120°F for low medium rare, 130°F for the upper end of medium rare, and 160°F for well done all the way through.
Cheap white buns suit thin burgers. Thicker, juicier burgers need a sturdier brioche-style bun.
Toppings are personal choice. Kenji likes onions and pickles and puts his toppings under the burger.

outline.title: Intro
outline.summary: Kenji, on his dock in Seattle, introduces a dozen ways to make hamburgers better.

outline.title: Tip 1: Use freshly ground beef
outline.summary: Compares supermarket packaged ground beef with freshly ground chuck from a butcher, explaining the texture and juiciness differences. Notes that most supermarkets will grind beef on request.

outline.title: Tip 2: Keep everything cold
outline.summary: Explains that warm meat lets fat soften and smear out, so the beef should go straight from the fridge into forming patties.

outline.title: Tip 3: Don't overhandle
outline.summary: Compares ground meat to bread dough: working it cross-links proteins and toughens the patty. Kenji shows how he forms patties on parchment on a tray.

outline.title: Tip 4: Don't salt or add anything to the meat
outline.summary: Argues against mix-ins like onions, parsley, breadcrumbs or eggs, and explains why salt mixed into the meat toughens the patty. Season only the outside.

outline.title: Tip 5: Keep patties consistent
outline.summary: Make patties the same size, by eye or with a scale, so they cook evenly and finish together.

outline.title: Tip 6: Shape matters
outline.summary: Thick patties get a center dimple to prevent bulging. Thin patties are pressed flat between parchment with a tray.

outline.title: Tip 7: Season liberally
outline.summary: Explains why salt is essential to flavor and recommends seasoning the outside generously with kosher salt and black pepper.

outline.title: Tip 8: Use a two-zone fire
outline.summary: Shows how to set up a two-zone fire on charcoal or gas grills. Covers using it to escape fat flare-ups and to finish thick burgers on the cool side with the lid on.

outline.title: Tip 9: Get good browning
outline.summary: Explains the Maillard reaction. Thick burgers brown on both sides, while thin burgers should be cooked about 90% on one side to avoid drying out.

outline.title: Tip 10: Use a thermometer
outline.summary: Recommends a thermometer over the poke test for home cooks and gives target temperatures from medium rare to well done.

outline.title: Tip 11: Choose your bun wisely
outline.summary: Cheap generic white buns suit thin burgers. Brioche-style supermarket buns hold up better for thick, juicy burgers.

outline.title: Tip 12: Toppings are personal choice
outline.summary: Kenji says toppings are up to you, names his own preferences (onions and pickles), and explains that he puts toppings under the burger.

outline.title: Outro
outline.summary: Wrap-up, a bite of the burger, pointers to more burger recipes on YouTube and Patreon, and a plug for his live show Tasting Notes in Seattle.
